exp.0:8:
God invites the priests to plead for his mercy, but he does so with irony: he tells them that what they offer came from their own hands. The source's phrase meaning to seek his favor is not carried over here, and the phrase meaning accepted is likewise left out. The question is this: will God grant them his favor if they treat him with such contempt?

The LORD speaks through the prophet Malachi, after the return from exile. The priests were offering animals that were blind, lame, or sick, something they would never dare to give to a governor. In this way they showed little respect for God.

For today: God does not seek what we have left over, but a sincere heart. Ask yourself what place you give him in your time, your money, and your attention, and offer him your best with gratitude and reverence.
exp.0:13:
It says the deceiver is cursed, that is, the one who has a healthy male in his flock and had promised it to God, but at the time of sacrifice gives a damaged or defective animal. "Cursed" means he is under God's judgment. God affirms the point: he is the Great King, and his name is dreadful, that is, worthy of respect and fear, among all the nations.

God speaks through the prophet Malachi, addressing a people who offered sacrifices out of habit, with reluctance. According to the law, the offerings had to be animals without defect. Offering the worst showed contempt for God, even though the appearance of worship was maintained.

For today: God deserves our best, not our leftovers. Ask yourself whether your time, your money and your attention to God come from the heart or are merely going through the motions. Keep what you promise, and give to him with gratitude.
exp.1:6:
This verse says that priests were to take care of and keep the knowledge of God on their lips. The people had to be able to come to them to learn the law, because the priest was a messenger (one who is sent) of the Lord of hosts, that is, of the Lord who rules over all.

God speaks through the prophet Malachi. First he recalls what Levi was like, the model of a good priest: he feared God, taught the truth, and turned many away from evil. Then he rebukes the priests of his time, who had strayed, caused the people to stumble, and showed partiality when applying the law.

Today, anyone who teaches or guides others, in the church or at home, must first live out and know the Word well. Before giving advice, ask yourself: am I speaking what God says, with humility and without favoritism?
exp.1:12:
The people covered the altar of the Lord with tears, weeping, and crying out, but God no longer looked upon their offerings or received them with pleasure. Here they were weeping, but God would not accept their worship.

The words come from God through the prophet Malachi. He accuses Judah of unfaithfulness: some were marrying women of foreign religion and abandoning the wife of their youth. The verses that follow make clear that disloyalty to one's spouse was a central part of the problem. God does not despise tears, but he does not accept them as a substitute for repentance.

For today: it is not enough to attend church, pray, or be moved emotionally if we mistreat those who are close to us. If there is a wound or failure in your marriage or family, seek reconciliation with humility, and then offer your worship to God with a clean heart.
exp.1:15:
The verse says that God hates divorce, that is, a man sending away his wife. It also says that whoever does this "covers his garment with violence," an image of violence or injustice that stays in plain sight, like a stain. That is why God warns: take heed to your spirit and do not deal treacherously.

God speaks through the prophet Malachi to a people who had returned from exile and had grown cold in their faith. Some men were abandoning the wife of their youth, with whom they had a covenant. There are several possible translations of this verse, but all of them express God's grief at betrayal.

For today: take care of your promises, above all in marriage. Examine your heart before coldness becomes disloyalty, and ask God for help to honor the one you pledged faithfulness to.
exp.2:0:
God announces that he will send a messenger to prepare the way before him. Then the Lord whom his people seek will suddenly come to his temple. He is also called "the messenger of the covenant," the one they say they delight in. The phrase "the messenger of the covenant" refers to the same messenger who prepares the way.

The Lord of hosts speaks through the prophet Malachi. The people doubted God's justice and lived with a cold faith. The verses that follow show that his coming purifies, not only comforts. Christians often see here John the Baptist and Jesus, as the New Testament does (Mark 1:2).

For today: it is not enough to say that we desire God; we must also let him cleanse us. Today, ask him to show you something you need to change, and take one concrete step of obedience.
exp.2:4:
God says he will come near to his people to judge them, and that he will be a swift witness against those who do harm. He names sorcerers (those who practice witchcraft), adulterers, those who swear falsely, those who hold back the wages of the day laborer (the worker paid by the day), and those who mistreat the widow, the fatherless, and the foreigner. All of this happens because they do not fear him.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Malachi, after the return from exile. Earlier he had announced that he would purify the sons of Levi, the way silver is refined. Now he shows that this cleansing also reaches the daily life of the people: how they treat others. His faithfulness is the reason the people have not been destroyed.

For today: examine how you treat those who depend on you, whether at work or at home. Pay what is fair, on time, and care for the weak. Reverence for God shows in how we treat other people.
exp.2:7:
God asks: "Will a man rob God?" And He Himself answers that His people have done exactly that. They act surprised and ask how they have robbed Him. God tells them: in tithes and offerings. The tithe was a tenth of what they earned, and the offerings were the first of the harvest, which was given to God.

God speaks through the prophet Malachi. His people, after returning from exile, had turned away from His commands and gave little or nothing for the temple and for those who served there. God invites them to return to Him, and He shows them a concrete example of that lack of commitment.

Today we can ask ourselves whether God holds first place in our money and in our time. More than a cold rule, it is an invitation to give with gratitude and trust, starting with the first and not with what is left over.
exp.2:10:
God promises that he will rebuke the devourer, that is, the pests or insects that destroy the harvests. This way the fruit of the land will not be spoiled, and the vine will not drop its grapes before they ripen (the phrase about losing its fruit early refers to the vine losing its fruit before the time).

The LORD speaks through the prophet Malachi, after the return from exile. The people had stopped bringing the tithes and the offerings to the temple, and God calls them to return to him. This promise was given to Israel under the covenant of the Law, so it should not be read as an automatic guarantee of wealth.

Today we can learn that God cares for those who trust in him. A practical application is to give faithfully and joyfully, and to trust that he will provide what we need, without demanding from him what we want.
exp.2:11:
Malachi says that when Israel returns to obeying God, the other nations will take notice. They will call Israel blessed, meaning happy and favored. A land that others admire, a pleasant country that people want, is what the verse describes. The nations here are the peoples who were not Israelites.

God himself speaks through the prophet Malachi. The people had returned from exile, but they had become careless: they held back the tithes and served God half-heartedly. God calls them to return to him and promises to care for their harvests. The people then answer with complaints, saying that serving God is pointless.

For today: obedience to God is not just keeping rules, but trusting in his care. You can begin with one concrete decision, such as being generous or faithful in something you have neglected, and letting God show his goodness in your life. Blessings are not always money.
exp.2:14:
This verse repeats what the people were saying bitterly: that the proud are happy and that wicked people prosper. They say that even those who put God to the test through their bad conduct went free without punishment. The proud are those who think highly of themselves, and to live without respect for God is to live in ungodliness.

The people of Israel are speaking, and God is confronting them through the prophet Malachi. They were people who felt that serving God was not worth the effort, because they saw that the wicked were doing well. God does not stay silent: he listens, and then shows that he remembers and cares for those who truly fear him, calling them his own special treasure.

For today: when it seems unfair that others prosper without living with integrity, do not grow bitter or stop serving God. Bring your complaint to him honestly, seek encouragement from other believers, and trust that God sees and remembers your faithfulness.
exp.3:1:
It says that for those who revere and honor God, the Sun of righteousness will rise, and will bring healing in his wings (his rays). "Healing" here means health or restoration. Those who receive it will go out full of joy, leaping like calves that go out free from the stall.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Malachi, at the end of the Old Testament. The people were discouraged and doubted that God would bring about justice. Just before this verse, God announces judgment on the proud and the wicked; here he promises comfort to the faithful. Many Christians see in the Sun of righteousness a sign of Christ, although the original text speaks of the day of the Lord in general.

When injustice wears you down, keep honoring God in your daily life. He sees the faithful and promises to heal and to give joy.
exp.3:2:
It says that the righteous will tread down the wicked, who will be turned to ashes under their feet. This will happen on the day that God himself is preparing. To tread down means to trample or crush. The soles of the feet are the bottoms of the feet.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Malachi to a discouraged people who doubted that God would bring about justice. He promises that there will be a day of judgment: the proud will be burned like stubble, and those who fear God will be healed and restored. Many understand the image of treading on the ashes as a picture of complete and certain victory; not everyone takes it literally.

For today: when you see that wickedness seems to be winning, do not grow bitter or take justice into your own hands. Keep honoring God with a faithful life, trusting that he has an appointed day to do justice.
exp.0:12:
God says that the people complained about serving Him: "Oh, what a nuisance!" They even turned up their noses at it. Moreover, instead of giving their best, they brought offerings that were stolen, lame, or sick. The word "stolen" means taken by theft, and God asks whether He will accept those offerings from their hands.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Malachi to Israel, after their return from exile. The priests and the people had become indifferent, and they gave God what was left over. Earlier, God had said that His name is great among the nations, and the contrast is strong: others honor Him, but His own people treat Him with reluctance. The following verse calls cursed the one who deceives God.

Today we might ask ourselves: do I give God my best time, attention, and generosity, or only the leftovers? Today you can set aside a quality moment to pray and serve Him gladly.
exp.0:2:
God says that He "hated" Esau, and that He turned his mountains into a wasteland and gave his inheritance to the desert jackals, wild animals that roam the wilderness. A "wasteland" means total ruin. Here "hated" probably means that God chose Jacob and not Esau, rather than a hatred like human hatred. Some understand it this way because of the Hebrew manner of speaking, which contrasts loving and hating.

God speaks through Malachi to a discouraged people after the exile, who doubted His love. He reminds them that He chose them, the descendants of Jacob, while Edom, the descendant of Esau, was left in ruin.

For today: when you doubt God's love, remember His faithfulness and His promises, not only your circumstances. His love is not measured by what you feel, but by what He has done and promised.
exp.2:13:
God quotes what the people have been saying: "It is futile to serve God." They ask what they have gained by keeping his requirements and by walking mournfully before the LORD of Hosts, that is, living in grief or humiliation, as in fasting or repentance. The word "futile" means "without result." "The LORD of Hosts" is a title of God as Lord over all power.

God speaks through the prophet Malachi, after the exile. The people were discouraged because they saw the wicked prospering and their hopes seeming to take a long time. Their complaint became harsh against God. Afterward, the text shows that some did fear God, and He listened to them and remembered them.

When obedience seems to bear no fruit, do not hide your discouragement or serve with bitterness. Bring it to God honestly, and remember that He sees and does not forget those who honor Him.
exp.2:15:
In a time when many people said that serving God was not worth it, there were people who did respect him and spoke with one another. God listened closely and heard them, and a scroll of remembrance was written before him for those who respected him and honored his name. The phrase "feared the LORD" means respecting and honoring him with reverence; the phrase "honored his name" means that they keep him in mind and value him.

The prophet Malachi speaks on God's behalf to a discouraged people. Some thought that the proud and the wicked fared better than the faithful. This verse shows God's answer: he sees those who continue to trust in him. It is debated whether that scroll is literal or a way of saying that God does not forget his own.

For today: when you become discouraged on seeing others prosper without obeying God, seek out sincere believers and talk together about your faith. God listens and does not forget the one who is faithful to him.
exp.0:7:
God asks the priests whether it is not wrong to offer him blind, lame, or sick animals. The word "governor" here means ruler or leader. God tells them: try offering that gift to your governor; would he be pleased with you, or show you favor? The phrases "pleased with" and "show you favor" mean welcomed kindly.

God himself speaks, through the prophet Malachi, to the priests of Israel. They were saying that the Lord's table was worthless, and they offered the worst they had, as if God did not deserve honor. God confronts them as both Father and Lord, and they pretend not to understand how they have offended him.

For today: let us give God our best and not the leftovers. This applies to our time, our money, our attention, and our service. God does not seek perfect things, but hearts that truly honor him.
exp.2:12:
God tells his people that their words against him have been harsh. "Your words against Me have been harsh," says the LORD. The people answer with feigned surprise, asking, "What have we spoken against You?" as though they did not know what he was accusing them of.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Malachi. The verses that follow show the problem: the people were saying that serving God was not worth the effort, and that the wicked seemed to prosper. These were complaints of the heart, yet God heard them as accusations against him.

For today: when life seems unfair, do not hide your doubts or dress them up. Bring them honestly and humbly before God, and ask him to help you trust him even when you do not understand everything.
exp.0:11:
God tells the priests that they "profane" his name, meaning they treat it as something common and worthless. They do this when they say that the altar is "defiled," meaning unworthy of respect, and that its food, the offerings, is "contemptible," something not worth bothering with.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Malachi, after the return from exile. The priests were offering animals that were lame, sick, or stolen, and they complained about how tiring the worship was. God contrasts this attitude with the nations, where his name is great. Scholars debate whether this speaks of the present or the future, but the rebuke is clear.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we give God our best or only what is left over. Our time, attention, and service matter. Worshiping with sincere gratitude, not out of mere obligation, honors his name.
exp.1:0:
This verse says that God speaks directly to the priests. The word "decree" here means a serious order or warning. The phrase "for you" means "meant for you," as if God were saying: "Now, priests, listen, this is for you."

The one speaking is the LORD, through the prophet Malachi. In the previous chapter, the priests had despised God's name by offering defective sacrifices and treating worship with indifference. Now God warns them that if they do not change and do not honor his name, consequences will come, which he describes as a curse upon their blessings.

For today: those of us who teach or serve in the church have a greater responsibility. It is worth asking ourselves whether we serve God with sincerity and reverence, or only out of habit, and asking him for a heart willing to honor him.
exp.0:5:
God gives two familiar examples: a son honors his father, and a servant respects his master. Then he asks: if I am a Father and a Master, where is the honor and respect due to me? To despise someone is to treat them as worthless or of little importance. Here, "fear" means reverence, a deep respect and awe. The priests respond with feigned surprise: "How have we despised your name?"

The LORD speaks through the prophet Malachi, after saying that he loves Israel. He addresses the priests, who were supposed to lead the people in worship. The verses that follow show the problem: they offered animals that were blind, lame, or sick, instead of the best.

For today: check whether you honor God only with words, or also with what you give him of your time, your money, and your attention. Offer him your best, not the leftovers.
exp.1:13:
This verse answers a question from the people: "Why does God not accept our offerings?" God says it is because He has been a witness to how each man was unfaithful to the wife of his youth. The wife of your youth is the wife you married when you were young. "Broken faith" means he broke his promise. She was his companion and his wife by a covenant, that is, a solemn promise made before God.

God speaks through the prophet Malachi to the people of Israel. The men kept up their religious rites in the temple, but many had abandoned their wives, probably through divorce. Some scholars think they also married women from other peoples who worshiped other gods, although the text does not say this with complete clarity.

For today: God values faithfulness in the home, not only religion on Sundays. Take care of your marriage, keep your promises, and treat your partner with respect and affection.
exp.2:17:
A time is coming when people will see clearly the difference between the one who lives righteously and the one who lives wickedly, between the one who serves God and the one who does not. The idea of turning back or changing one's mind is not part of this verse, so the focus is simply that people will come to see the difference clearly.

God speaks through the prophet Malachi. The people were discouraged and said that it was pointless to serve God, since the wicked seemed to prosper (Malachi 3:14-15). God answers that he remembers those who fear him, calls them his cherished treasure, and promises that in the end it will be seen who is who. Interpreters differ on whether this refers to the final judgment or to a nearer time.

For today: when it seems that serving God brings no result, do not lose heart. Remain faithful with humility, trusting that God sees, remembers, and will make the truth clear in his time.
exp.1:10:
This verse says that the people of Judah were unfaithful to God. "Broken faith" means that they betrayed their commitment to him. An "abomination" is something God hates. Judah "profaned" what is holy, which means they treated as common what belongs to the LORD and what he loves. The phrase about marrying "the daughter of a foreign god" refers to a woman who worshiped another god.

The prophet Malachi speaks, giving God's message to a people who had returned from exile. God rebukes them because they were breaking the covenant. Many understand that the main problem was joining themselves to women who followed other gods, which turned the people's hearts away. Some also see here a broader theme of disloyalty, since the text that follows mentions tears and divorces.

For today: be careful about the decisions that most shape your faith, such as your friendships, your marriage, and your commitments. Ask God that your loyalty to him would guide your most important choices.
exp.0:4:
The explanation says that the people of Israel will see with their own eyes how God acts, and that they will then declare his greatness. The verse's words "even beyond the borders of Israel" can be understood as meaning that his greatness would be seen even outside his land, that is, that he would be recognized even beyond Israel.

God speaks through the prophet Malachi. The people doubted his love, and God reminds them that he chose Israel. Edom, a descendant of Esau, lay in ruins and could not rebuild. Then God rebukes the priests for offering unworthy sacrifices.

For today: when you doubt God's love, remember what he has done for you and answer him with gratitude, giving him your best and not what is left over.
exp.1:2:
God says he will rebuke the descendants of the priests. Some read "descendants" as offspring, while others read it as the harvest. Then he says he will spread dung on their faces, meaning the waste left over from the animals offered in their sacrifices. The feasts they hold are the religious festivals they celebrate, and the waste from those feasts is what he will spread on them. In the end, they will be carried off along with that waste, cast out together with it.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Malachi. The priests were offering sacrifices without reverence or sincerity, and they dishonored his name. Before this punishment, he gave them a warning: if they did not repent, their blessings would turn into a curse. He wanted them to return to the covenant of reverence that Levi had kept.

For today: God is not pleased with a religion of appearances. Before you serve, sing, or give anything, examine your heart and ask him to let your worship come from sincere reverence.
exp.1:1:
God warns that if the priests do not listen and do not take it to heart to honor his name, he will send a curse upon them. He will even curse their blessings, that is, the good things they have received and the blessings they pronounce over the people. To take something to heart means to take it seriously and settle on it in your mind and will. God says he has already begun to curse them.

The Lord of hosts speaks through the prophet Malachi. He addresses the priests, who were treating God with careless offerings and teaching that fell short. God reminds them of his covenant with Levi, the priestly tribe. Interpreters may differ in how they understand "I will curse your blessings," but the general meaning is that their religious service would lose God's favor.

For today: it is not enough to carry out rituals or to serve in the church. God looks at the heart. Ask yourself whether your service, your work, and your prayer come from a sincere desire to honor him.
exp.2:5:
He says that God does not change: He is always the same in His character and in His promises. Because of this, the descendants of Jacob, that is, the people of Israel, have not been destroyed. The phrase "I do not change" means "I do not change" in the sense of "I remain the same."

Here the Lord speaks through the prophet Malachi. He has just announced judgment against injustice and disrespect toward God. Even so, the people are still standing, and the verse attributes this to God's faithfulness, not to their deserving it. Then He calls them to return to Him.

For today: if you have failed and feel that God has already grown tired of you, remember that His patience does not depend on your constancy, but on His steadfast character. His faithfulness invites you to return today, right now, with sincerity.
exp.1:5:
Malachi 2:6 says that Levi, the ancestor of the priests, taught true instruction and never let anything false pass his lips. He walked with God in peace and uprightness, meaning in harmony and righteousness, and he turned many people away from doing wrong.

The prophet Malachi, speaking for God, addresses the priests of Israel after the return from exile. He reminds them of the covenant with Levi and the example he left, in order to set it against their carelessness. The verses that follow accuse them of turning from the path and causing others to stumble. Scholars debate whether "Levi" refers to the man himself or to the whole priestly tribe.

For today: whoever teaches or influences others, such as parents, teachers, or leaders, should strive to make their words and their lives agree. Ask God that your example may help others draw near to Him.
exp.3:5:
It says that a messenger, called here "Elijah the prophet," will turn the hearts of the fathers to their children, and the hearts of the children to their fathers. In this way God will keep from having to come and strike the land with a curse. "Turn" means to bring back, to restore; striking with a curse means bringing total judgment.

God speaks through the prophet Malachi, at the end of the Old Testament. He calls the people to remember the law of Moses and announces the messenger before "the day of the LORD." The New Testament connects this promise with John the Baptist (Luke 1:17), though some also see a future fulfillment in it.

For today: seek reconciliation in your family. Take the first step with a phone call, an apology, or quality time together. God wants homes where there is forgiveness, open conversation, and shared faith.
exp.0:10:
He says that God's name will be great among the nations, from where the sun rises to where it sets. In every place, incense and pure offerings are presented in his name. The word "nations" in the verse refers to the peoples who were not Israel.

God himself speaks, through the prophet Malachi. He rebukes the priests of Israel, who offered animals that were lame, sick, or stolen, and who treated worship with indifference. By contrast, he says that his name is honored among the nations. Some believe he is speaking of sincere worshipers from other nations in that time; others believe he is announcing a future in which everyone will worship him.

For today: God deserves the best, not the leftovers. Examine how you pray, give, and serve. Do it with sincerity and gratitude, not just to fulfill an obligation.
exp.3:4:
God promises to send the prophet Elijah before "the day of the Lord," a moment of judgment and justice that will be great and awesome. The phrase "I will send you" means that God is sending this messenger to his people. "Awesome" here means that it inspires deep respect and wonder.

The one speaking is God, through Malachi, to the people of Israel after the exile. Many had grown cold in their faith. God asks them to remember the law of Moses and promises a messenger who will prepare them. In the New Testament, Jesus said that John the Baptist fulfilled this role (Matthew 11:14). Some believers also see another future fulfillment; opinions vary.

For today: God warns in love before he judges. If there is something you need to put right with him or with your family, do not leave it for later. Today you can ask for forgiveness, return to the Word, and seek reconciliation.
exp.3:0:
A day of judgment is coming, burning like a furnace. All the arrogant and everyone who does evil will be like stubble, which is dry straw or stalks that burn up quickly. That day will set them on fire and consume them completely. The statement that nothing will be left to them, not a root or a branch, means that nothing of them will remain.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Malachi, near the end of the Old Testament. The people doubted God's justice and thought that the wicked were doing well. God answers that there will be a day when He will set everything right. The verses that follow show the contrast: healing and joy for those who honor Him.

For today: do not let yourself be discouraged when injustice seems to win. Trust that God will judge with perfect justice, and live with humility, seeking to honor Him every day.
exp.1:14:
This verse is difficult, and scholars explain it in several ways. Here the LORD asks whether he did not make them one, since he had a portion of the Spirit and could have made many. The reason he gives is that he seeks godly offspring, that is, families that honor him. That is why he warns: guard yourselves in your spirit and do not break faith with the wife of your youth. "Youth" means the early years of life, and "break faith" means to be unfaithful or to betray a trust.

God speaks through the prophet Malachi. The people had returned from exile, several men were abandoning their wives, and God no longer welcomed their offerings.

For today: marriage is a covenant before God, not merely an agreement between two people. If there are tensions in your home, guard your heart, be faithful in small things, and seek reconciliation before separation.
exp.2:16:
God says that those who fear him will be his, a very special treasure to him. He speaks of "the day when I prepare My treasured possession," a day on which he will act. Then he will treat them with compassion, like a father who shows mercy to a son who serves him. The phrase "I will spare them" means "I will forgive them," and here it carries the sense of treating them with mercy and caring for them.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Malachi. The people were discouraged and said that the wicked were doing better than the faithful. Some who did fear God encouraged one another, and God listened to them and recorded them in a book of remembrance. This promise is his answer: he has not forgotten them. Scholars understand "the day" in different ways, as either a coming judgment or the final day.

For today: when serving God seems not worth the effort, encourage yourself with other believers and trust that God sees your faithfulness and regards you as his own.
exp.1:9:
Malachi 2:10 asks whether we do not all have one Father, and whether one God did not create us all. It then asks why we break faith with one another and so violate the covenant of our ancestors. Breaking faith means being disloyal to someone or treating them with little regard. To profane something means to break or violate what is sacred.

The one speaking is the prophet Malachi, who brings God's message to a people who had returned from exile. The priests were teaching without justice, and the people were not faithful to one another. The verses that follow speak of marrying women who worshiped other gods. Some think it also refers to divorcing Israelite wives, although that becomes clearer later.

For today: if God is the Father of all believers, we cannot treat anyone in the family of faith with contempt or disloyalty. Today you can guard your words and keep your commitments to others.
exp.0:0:
This verse is the introduction to the book. "Burden" means a heavy message, a serious warning that God commands to be delivered. It is "the word of the LORD," meaning the LORD himself speaks, and he speaks "to Israel," that is, with a correction directed at his people. "Through Malachi" means he passes it on through that prophet. The name Malachi can be translated "my messenger."

God is the one speaking, and Malachi is only the spokesman. We know almost nothing about the author, and the exact date is debated, though many place it after the return from exile. Right away, God reminds them of his love, but the people respond with doubt and coldness.

For today: before reacting to a correction from God, remember that it comes from someone who loves you. Read his Word with humility, without becoming defensive, and let him teach you.
exp.2:3:
He says that when God has finished purifying his people, the offerings of Judah and Jerusalem will please him, as they did in days of old and in years gone by. The word "please" here means something pleasing or delightful, like a fragrance that is welcome.

God speaks through the prophet Malachi. The people were offering sacrifices half-heartedly and unfairly. God announces that he will come like a refining fire and like soap that cleanses, to purify the priests, the sons of Levi. After that cleansing, their worship will once again please him. Christians often also see here a preparation for the work of Christ, although the text speaks first of Israel.

For today: God cares more about a clean heart and a righteous life than about the mere outward act of religion. Ask him to examine you and purify you, and then serve and give sincerely, treating others well.
exp.0:1:
God begins by telling his people, "I have loved you." They answer with doubt, "How have You loved us?" God reminds them that Esau and Jacob were brothers, and yet he chose Jacob. The word "hated," as used here, is usually understood to mean preferring or not choosing, not hatred in the sense of human resentment.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Malachi to Israel, which had returned from exile and was discouraged and spiritually cold. God reminds them of his covenant. Edom, descended from Esau, suffered ruin, and although it wants to rebuild, it will not succeed. Some see here a theme of the choosing of nations, not of personal salvation.

When you doubt God's love, do not be guided only by your circumstances. Remember the times when he sustained you, forgave you, and cared for you. Give thanks for that love you did not deserve.
exp.1:11:
God says he will cut off from among his people, "the tents of Jacob," anyone who does this. To "cut off" means to remove or eliminate. The phrase "everyone who is awake and aware" points to people who know what they are doing and do it anyway. The word "offering" refers to a gift brought to God, and the verse says the LORD will cut off even the one who brings it.

The prophet Malachi speaks in God's name to a people who had returned from exile. Judah had been unfaithful to the covenant: some were marrying women who worshiped other gods, and the verses that follow speak of betraying the wife of one's youth. Even so, they continued bringing offerings to the altar.

Today, God is not pleased with a religion that is only outward. He desires faithfulness in the home and in our commitments. Today you can examine whether your treatment of your family matches what you say you believe.
exp.2:9:
God invites his people to bring the full tithe into the storehouse, a store room beside the temple, so that there may be food in God's house. Then he challenges them: "Test me in this," that is, put me to the test. He promises to open the windows of heaven, an image of abundant rain, and to pour out blessing without measure.

God speaks through the prophet Malachi, after the return from exile. He accuses Israel of robbing him by withholding the tithes and the offerings, and because of this the nation was suffering shortage. The priests and Levites depended on those offerings. The call is to return to God with trust and obedience.

For today: Christians debate whether the tithe applies in the same way now, but the principle remains. Give faithfully and joyfully, planning your generosity, and trust that God cares for you. Do not use it as a method for gaining wealth.
exp.0:3:
What the passage says: The Edomites, descendants of Esau, say that they have been devastated and that they will rebuild the ruins. God answers that, although they may build, he will demolish. Their land will be called "The Land of Wickedness," and they are a people with whom the LORD is indignant forever.

Context: The LORD speaks through Malachi to a discouraged Israel, who doubted his love. God reminds them that he chose Jacob and not Esau. Edom is an example of judgment on those who live turned away from God. Some think that the phrase "I hated" expresses a lesser choice, not human hatred; scholars debate the exact nuance.

For today: We can trust God's love even when life is hard. And the projects we raise without taking him into account have no secure foundation; it is wise to build with him.
exp.1:4:
God says that he made a covenant, a solemn promise, with Levi, and that he gave Levi life and peace. Those things were a gift to him. The reverence described here is not a paralyzing dread but a deep respect toward God. Levi revered God and stood in awe of his name, meaning he lived with humility and reverence.

God, speaking through the prophet Malachi, addresses the priests of his time. They were not carrying out their service well, and God rebukes them with strong words. He reminds them of how a priest ought to be, using Levi, the ancestor of the priests, as an example. Some understand "Levi" as the person, and others as the whole tribe.

For today: if God has entrusted you with something, whether in the church, in your family, or at work, do it with reverence toward him and with humility. That sincere attitude is what God blesses.
exp.1:8:
God says that, because of the priests' failure, He has made them despised and humiliated before all the people. The reason is that they did not keep His ways, meaning they did not live as He taught. On top of that, they showed partiality in matters of the law: they applied the law with favoritism, treating some people better than others.

God speaks through the prophet Malachi. The priests were meant to teach the law faithfully, but they turned from the right path and caused many to stumble. So God takes away the respect they should have had. Their lack of integrity had public consequences.

For today: those who teach or guide others, whether in the church or at home, carry a greater responsibility. We can ask God to help us live out what we teach and to treat everyone with justice, without favoritism.
exp.1:7:
God accuses the priests of having turned away from the right path. They did not go wrong alone: through their faulty teaching they caused many others to stumble. The phrase "violated the covenant of Levi" means they broke the special commitment God made with the priestly tribe. To "cause to stumble" means to bring about the failure of others.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Malachi, after the return from exile. Earlier he describes what a faithful priest was like: he taught the truth, lived in peace and righteousness, and turned many away from evil. The priests of the prophet's time, by contrast, were not living up to that calling, and the verses that follow say they showed partiality toward some over others.

For today: if you teach or guide others, whether in the church, the family, or at work, take care that your life and your words go together. Your example can help others walk with God, or cause them to stumble.
exp.3:3:
God tells his people to remember the law he gave through Moses, whom he calls "my servant." He gave that law at Horeb, another name for Mount Sinai. The statutes and ordinances are the commands and rules he gave for all of Israel. To remember also means to obey.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Malachi, in the last message of the Old Testament. Before this, he promises justice and healing for those who fear him; afterward, he announces Elijah before the day of the Lord. Between these two promises he places this call: while they wait, they must stay faithful to his word.

For today: while we wait for the Lord, being moved by his promises is not enough. Set aside a fixed time each week to read his Word, and practice one concrete thing it tells you.
exp.0:6:
God accuses the priests of presenting defiled food on his altar, that is, offerings that are impure or unworthy. They ask, "How have we defiled You?" and God answers that they have done so by saying that the table of the LORD is contemptible, something of little worth.

Speaking through the prophet Malachi, God addresses the priests of Israel. They were offering blind, lame, or sick animals, as the following verses show, and they kept the best for themselves. In this they showed little respect for God. He reminds them that a son honors his father, and they were not honoring him.

For today: God deserves our best, not our leftovers. We can ask ourselves whether we give him our best time, attention, and resources, or only what remains, and worship him with a sincere and grateful heart.
exp.2:8:
The verse says that the whole nation is under a curse because they are still robbing God. The phrase "You are cursed with a curse" means that they are suffering the consequences of their disobedience, as God had warned in the law. "Storehouse" is a place where goods are kept, and "firstfruits" were the first produce offered to God.

God speaks through the prophet Malachi, after the return from exile. The people had grown cold spiritually and were not bringing the tithes and offerings that supported the temple and the Levites. God calls them to return to him and promises care and blessing if they do. Scholars agree on the general situation, though not on every detail of the difficulties the people were facing.

For today: honestly examine whether God holds first place in your time, your money, and your heart. Giving with gratitude, according to your means, is a way of trusting him and not merely keeping a rule.
exp.0:9:
This verse says that God would rather someone shut the doors of the temple than keep up offerings that are made without sincerity. The phrase "useless fires" means fires that accomplish nothing and bring no benefit. "Kindle useless fires on My altar" refers to lighting the fire on the altar for offerings that God does not value. The "offering" is the gift presented. God says he takes no pleasure in them and will accept nothing brought from their hands.

God speaks through the prophet Malachi, after the return from exile. The priests were offering animals that were blind, lame, or sick, that is, the worst they had, and they treated worship with contempt. God challenges them: they would never offer such a thing to a governor. Some understand the doors and the fire as services that were carried out without love.

For today: it is not about giving much, but about giving with sincerity. Ask yourself whether you give God the best of your time, attention, and resources, or only what is left over. Today you can offer him something with gratitude and from the heart.
exp.2:2:
This verse says that the Lord will act like a craftsman who sits down to refine silver. He heats the metal to remove the impurities and leave it pure. In this way he will purify the sons of Levi, that is, the priests and servants of the temple, and refine them like gold and silver, so that they will present offerings to the Lord in righteousness.

The verse uses the word "refiner," and "purifier" means one who makes something clean.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Malachi. The people had become careless in their faith and in how they treated one another. God announces that he will come to cleanse first those who led the worship. Many Christians see here a reference to John the Baptist and to Christ, although there is discussion about how all of this is fulfilled.

For today: when God corrects us or puts us through trials, it is not to destroy us, but to purify us. We can pray, "Lord, remove what is left over in my heart," and seek to live with honesty and righteousness.
exp.2:1:
It says that when the Lord comes to his temple, no one will easily be able to endure that moment. His presence is like a refiner's fire, which removes the impurities from metal, and like a launderer's soap, a strong product used to clean cloth. The word "endure" here means to bear up under or to stand firm.

The prophet Malachi speaks on God's behalf. The people doubted God's justice and lived with a cold faith, even the priests. God promises to send a messenger and then to come himself. Many Christians see here John the Baptist and Jesus; others emphasize only the original meaning for Israel. Its purpose is to purify the sons of Levi so that they may offer sincere worship.

For today: when God confronts us, it is not to destroy us, but to purify us. We can ask him with humility to remove whatever harms our heart.
exp.2:6:
God tells the Israelites that, from the days of their ancestors, they have turned away from his statutes and have not kept them. Even so, he invites them: "Return to Me," that is, come back to Me, "and I will return to you." They answer with a question: "How can we return?" as if they did not see their own failure.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Malachi, after the exile. He has just said that he does not change, and for that reason his people were not destroyed. His faithfulness is what makes the invitation possible. Then he will point to a specific failure: they were not bringing the tithes and the offerings.

For today: returning to God begins with honesty. Instead of asking "What have I done wrong?" as a way of defending ourselves, we can ask him to show us what needs to be corrected, trusting that he welcomes whoever comes back.
exp.1:16:
The explanation says that the people have wearied God, that is, they have worn him out and tried his patience, with their words. They act innocent and ask: "How have we wearied him?" God answers: by saying that all who do evil are good in his sight, and that he delights in them. They also mockingly ask: "Where is the God of justice?"

Malachi speaks for God after the return from exile. The people were disillusioned, and there was disloyalty, even within marriages. Seeing that the wicked seemed to prosper, some doubted God's justice. Scholars understand in different ways whether they said this with irony or with genuine doubt, but God takes it as an offense.

For today: when injustice discourages you, bring your complaint to God with humility and sincerity, without accusing him of approving evil. Trust that he is just, even when his answer is slow in coming.
exp.1:3:
God says that when the priests see the consequences of their disobedience, they will understand that He sent this warning to them. His purpose was that His covenant with Levi, the tribe of the priests, would continue. "Will know" means "will recognize." "Lord of Hosts" speaks of God's power over all.

God speaks through the prophet Malachi to the priests of Israel, who were serving carelessly and without reverence in the temple. He warns them of a curse if they do not change. Then he recalls Levi, who honored God, taught the truth, and turned many away from evil. That was the model they were meant to follow.

For today: God corrects because He wants to restore His relationship with us, not merely to punish. We can ask ourselves whether our service to God is sincere or just a habit, and ask Him for a heart that truly honors Him.

sum.1: God rebukes the priests for not honoring his name, for turning aside from the law and causing many to stumble, and he warns them of a curse. He also condemns the faithlessness of the people: marrying women who worship other gods and abandoning the wife of their youth. Furthermore, he accuses them of wearying him by saying that God takes pleasure in evil.
sum.3: Malachi 4 announces that the day of the Lord is coming: a burning day that will destroy the proud and all who do evil. For those who fear his name, the Sun of righteousness will rise with healing in its wings, and they will leap for joy. God asks them to remember the law of Moses, and he promises to send Elijah to turn the hearts of fathers and children toward each other.
sum.2: God promises to send a messenger and then come to his temple to purify his people and judge injustice. He calls Israel to return to him, to be faithful with the tithes, and to trust in his blessing. He also promises that those who fear him will be his special treasure.
sum.0: God reminds Israel that he has loved them, but the people doubt it. He then rebukes the priests because, instead of honoring him as Father and Lord, they bring him blind, lame, or sick animals. God says that his name is great among the nations and that he deserves the best.
